# The `sf` object {#sec-m2-sf}

`sf` (*simple features*) is the standard for vector data in R. The central idea is simple and
solves half of geoprocessing problems: **an `sf` object is a `data.frame` with a
geometry column**. Everything you learned in module 1 (`filter`, `mutate`, `summarise`,
`join`) still applies, and the geometry follows along through the operations.

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r}
sf::sf_extSoftVersion()
```

These are the libraries that do the heavy lifting: GDAL (reading/writing formats),
PROJ (projections) and GEOS (geometric operations). They are the same ones QGIS uses underneath. R
is not a "weaker" alternative: it is the same machine with a different interface.

## Building geometries by hand

To understand the structure, it is worth building each type of geometry once. We will use real ports
as the example.

```{r}
# point
porto <- sf::st_point(c(-48.5, -25.5))
class(porto)

# from a table of coordinates: the most common case day to day.
# instead of typing the coordinates by hand, we read a real file with
# the location of port facilities from ANTAQ's register
portos_tab <- readr::read_csv("dados/portos_antaq.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
portos_tab

portos <- sf::st_as_sf(portos_tab, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
portos
```

Read carefully the header `sf` prints: number of features, geometry type,
dimension, `bbox` (bounding box) and the **CRS**. It is the first thing to check in any
spatial dataset.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Before the first map: choose a basemap that does not need an API key

Some options in `mapview`'s default list (such as those from Stadia Maps) now require registration and
an API key. To avoid this, set once, at the start of the session, a list of free
basemaps with no registration:

```{r}
mapview::mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery"))
```

This option applies to every `mapview()` in the session, including those in this chapter.
:::

```{r}
mapview::mapview(portos)
```

`mapview()` is the quickest way to check whether spatial data are where they should be: an
interactive map, with zoom and attribute popups, from any `sf` object. We come back to it
in every chapter of this module, whenever there is a spatial result to check.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Large datasets make `mapview()` slow

With many features (a whole set of municipal boundaries, a road network), the default `mapview()` can
freeze the browser. The `leafgl` package renders the same thing with WebGL, much faster.
Just install `leafgl` and switch the drawing platform once, at the start of the session:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("leafgl")
mapview::mapviewOptions(platform = "leafgl")
```

After that, every `mapview::mapview(objeto_sf)` in the session uses `leafgl` automatically.
:::

```{r}
class(portos)
sf::st_geometry_type(portos, by_geometry = FALSE)
sf::st_bbox(portos)
sf::st_crs(portos)$input
```

`st_as_sf()` with `coords =` is probably the function you will use most: it turns
any spreadsheet with latitude and longitude into spatial data.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The order is longitude, latitude

`coords = c("lon", "lat")`: **x first**. Reversed, your points land in the Indian Ocean or
in Antarctica. When the map comes out empty or with absurd points, this is the first suspect.
:::

### Lines and polygons

```{r}
# line: a sequence of points
trecho <- sf::st_linestring(rbind(
  c(-48.51, -25.50),
  c(-48.80, -25.42),
  c(-49.27, -25.43)
))

# polygon: closed ring (first point = last point)
quadra <- sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(
  c(-48.6, -25.6), c(-48.4, -25.6),
  c(-48.4, -25.4), c(-48.6, -25.4),
  c(-48.6, -25.6)
)))

sf::st_sfc(trecho, quadra, crs = 4326) |> sf::st_geometry_type()
sf::st_length(sf::st_sfc(trecho, crs = 4326))
sf::st_area(sf::st_sfc(quadra, crs = 4326))
```

```{r}
mapview::mapview(sf::st_sfc(trecho, crs = 4326), color = "#1a5b8a") +
  mapview::mapview(sf::st_sfc(quadra, crs = 4326), col.regions = "#e07b39")
```

Notice that `st_length()` and `st_area()` return the result **with units** (metres, square
metres). `sf` uses the `units` package. This prevents the classic mistake of reporting area in
decimal degrees:

```{r}
area <- sf::st_area(sf::st_sfc(quadra, crs = 4326))
units::set_units(area, km^2)
as.numeric(units::set_units(area, km^2))   # to use in a calculation or chart
```

### Geometry types

| Type | What it is | Example in our context |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `POINT` | one point | port facility, counting station, bus stop |
| `MULTIPOINT` | several points in one feature | set of entrances to a terminal |
| `LINESTRING` | one line | highway segment, railway line |
| `MULTILINESTRING` | several lines in one feature | a whole highway, with discontinuous segments |
| `POLYGON` | one area | municipality, census tract, catchment area |
| `MULTIPOLYGON` | several areas in one feature | municipality with islands, state with enclaves |
| `GEOMETRYCOLLECTION` | a mix of types | result of some intersections |

In practice, IBGE boundaries come as `MULTIPOLYGON` and road networks as
`MULTILINESTRING`, because a feature can be physically discontinuous. When a function
requires a specific type, convert:

```{r}
#| eval: false
sf::st_cast(x, "POLYGON")        # splits each part into a row of the table
sf::st_cast(x, "MULTIPOLYGON")   # groups them
sf::st_collection_extract(x, "POLYGON")   # discards what is not a polygon
```

## Reading files

`st_read()` reads practically any vector format. GDAL decides based on what it recognises in the
extension.

```{r}
#| eval: false
sf::st_read("dados/brutos/snv/SNV_202601A.shp")      # Shapefile
sf::st_read("dados/brutos/base.gpkg", layer = "rodovias")  # GeoPackage (several layers)
sf::st_read("dados/brutos/limites.geojson")
sf::st_read("dados/brutos/base.sqlite", layer = "portos")  # SQLite/Spatialite
sf::st_layers("dados/brutos/base.gpkg")              # which layers exist in the file
```

Arguments that solve the most frequent problems:

```{r}
#| eval: false
sf::st_read("arquivo.shp", quiet = TRUE)                 # without the reading message
sf::st_read("arquivo.shp", options = "ENCODING=LATIN1")  # accents in an old shapefile
sf::st_read("arquivo.shp", query = "SELECT * FROM arquivo WHERE sg_uf = 'PR'")  # filters while reading
sf::st_read("arquivo.gpkg", wkt_filter = sf::st_as_text(sf::st_geometry(area)))         # spatial crop
```

The last two matter with large datasets: instead of loading 500 MB of national boundaries only to
filter one state afterwards, the filter goes along with the reading.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Shapefile or GeoPackage?

The Shapefile (`.shp`) is the most widespread format, but it has real limitations: it is 4 to 6 files
that must travel together, column names limited to 10 characters, and problems with
accents. The **GeoPackage** (`.gpkg`) is a single file, without these limits, with several
layers inside. For working files and results, use `.gpkg`; keep `.shp` only
when the recipient requires it.
:::

## Writing

```{r}
#| eval: false
dir.create("resultados", showWarnings = FALSE)

sf::st_write(portos, "resultados/portos.gpkg", delete_dsn = TRUE)   # overwrites the file
sf::st_write(portos, "resultados/portos.shp")
sf::st_write(portos, "resultados/portos.geojson")

# several layers in the same GeoPackage
sf::st_write(portos,  "resultados/analise.gpkg", layer = "portos")
sf::st_write(trechos, "resultados/analise.gpkg", layer = "trechos", append = TRUE)

# table without geometry, for Excel
portos |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> writexl::write_xlsx("resultados/portos.xlsx")

# coordinates as columns
portos |> dplyr::mutate(lon = sf::st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1],
                 lat = sf::st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2]) |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  readr::write_csv("resultados/portos.csv")
```

`st_drop_geometry()` is the shortcut back to an ordinary `data.frame`. It is useful when the geometry
has done its job and you just want the table.

## `dplyr` verbs on `sf` objects

```{r}
portos |>
  dplyr::filter(uf %in% c("PR", "SC")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(regiao = "Sul") |>
  dplyr::select(nome, uf, regiao)
```

The geometry is "sticky": it survives `filter`, `mutate`, `select` and `arrange` without you
asking. Two exceptions worth knowing. Note that, on `sf` objects, grouping is done
with `group_by()`, not with module 1's `.by` argument, which the `sf` method does not implement:

```{r}
# summarise aggregates the geometries (union) within each group
portos |>
  dplyr::group_by(uf) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n()) |>
  sf::st_geometry_type()
```

```{r}
# to aggregate ONLY the attributes, remove the geometry first
portos |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::count(uf)
```

## Quick inspection of a new spatial dataset

The routine worth running whenever you open an unknown file. To keep it concrete,
we apply it straight to the `portos` object we already have: in your case, start by replacing the first line with
`x <- sf::st_read("arquivo.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)`.

```{r}
x <- portos

nrow(x)                          # how many features
sf::st_geometry_type(x, by_geometry = FALSE)  # what type of geometry
sf::st_crs(x)$input                  # which coordinate system
sf::st_bbox(x)                       # where it is (as expected?)
names(x)                         # which attributes
all(sf::st_is_valid(x))              # is the geometry valid?
mapview::mapview(x)                  # does the drawing make sense?
```

`st_is_valid()` deserves attention: invalid geometries (self-intersections, reversed rings) are
common in old shapefiles and make later operations fail with obscure messages.
The fix is one line:

```{r}
#| eval: false
x <- sf::st_make_valid(x)
```
